--- title: "Group analysis" subtitle: "Second-level inference over first-level estimates, fully typed." jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: auto --- This is the last stage of the workflow. A first-level model gives you one effect estimate per subject; a *second-level* (group) analysis asks whether that effect holds across subjects, and how it varies with subject-level variables. Per-subject estimates flow into a `GroupData` container and out through result objects you read by attribute. The group design is written as a formula, the same way you would write it in R or statsmodels. Three functions in `fmrimod.stats` cover this stage. They are the same underlying model seen from different angles, so pick by what you want back: - **`fmri_meta`** — the workhorse. Meta-analysis when the formula is `~ 1`; meta-regression when you add a covariate (`~ 1 + C(group)`). Returns an `FmriMetaResult`. - **`fmri_ttest`** — a thin shortcut for the plain one-sample *t*-test, when that is literally all you want. Returns an `FmriTTestResult`. - **`group_fit`** — one canonical door that *always* returns the same `GroupFitResult`, whatever model you ask for. Worth it when many fits must come back as one uniform type (a sweep, a pipeline stage). If you only read one section, read `fmri_meta` below — it is enough for almost every analysis. ## Per-Subject Estimates → Typed `GroupData` A second-level analysis starts from one effect (and its standard error) per subject per feature. Stack them as a tidy frame and let `group_data_from_csv` build the typed container — it accepts an in-memory DataFrame and a covariate table, so the group design is declared by data, not assembled by hand. ::: {#cda134e1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import fmrimod as fm from fmrimod.dataset import group_data_from_csv from fmrimod.stats import fmri_meta, group_fit, GroupFitRequest, fmri_ttest rng = np.random.default_rng(12) n_subj, n_feat = 10, 6 subjects = [f"s{i + 1}" for i in range(n_subj)] group = np.repeat(["ctrl", "patient"], n_subj // 2) # Synthetic first-level betas + sampling variances (the fixture only). true = np.array([[0.2] * n_feat, [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.0, -0.1, -0.2]]) V = rng.uniform(0.04, 0.12, size=(n_subj, n_feat)) gnum = (group == "patient").astype(int) Y = np.column_stack([np.ones(n_subj), gnum]) @ true + rng.normal(scale=np.sqrt(V)) long = pd.DataFrame([ {"subject": s, "roi": f"feature_{j + 1}", "beta": Y[i, j], "se": np.sqrt(V[i, j])} for i, s in enumerate(subjects) for j in range(n_feat) ]) gd = group_data_from_csv( long, effect_cols={"beta": "beta", "se": "se"}, subject_col="subject", roi_col="roi", covariates=pd.DataFrame({"group": group}), ) gd.format, len(gd.subjects) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ('csv', 10) ``` ::: ::: ## One-Sample Random Effects The common second-level question — "is the effect non-zero across subjects?" — is a random-effects meta-analysis with an intercept-only formula. `fmri_meta` returns a typed `FmriMetaResult`: read `.coefficients`, `.p`, `.tau2` as attributes. ::: {#baa34a78 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} one = fmri_meta(gd, formula="~ 1", method="pm") pd.DataFrame({ "feature": one.feature_names, "estimate": one.coefficients[:, 0], "p": one.p[:, 0], "tau2": one.tau2, }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
feature estimate p tau2
0 roi=feature_1 0.412 0.000 0.042
1 roi=feature_2 0.337 0.000 0.001
2 roi=feature_3 0.302 0.001 0.000
3 roi=feature_4 0.256 0.011 0.018
4 roi=feature_5 0.100 0.245 0.004
5 roi=feature_6 -0.044 0.617 0.000
``` ::: ::: ## One Result Type for Every Fit: `group_fit` `fmri_meta` and `fmri_ttest` each return their own result type. When you run many second-level models and want them all to come back as the *same* object, `group_fit` is the single entry that always returns a `GroupFitResult`. Called on a dataset alone, it runs **one explicit default**: a one-sample (`formula="~ 1"`) **random-effects meta-analysis**, with Paule–Mandel `tau2` and inverse-variance weights. That is the same model as `fmri_meta(gd, formula="~ 1", method="pm")` — `group_fit(gd)` is just the uniform-result-type door to it. ::: {#0cbad2a6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} res = group_fit(gd) type(res).__name__, res.method, res.backend, res.estimate[:, 0].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ('GroupFitResult', 'pm', 'python', array([ 0.412, 0.337, 0.302, 0.256, 0.1 , -0.044])) ``` ::: ::: For anything other than that default, pass a `GroupFitRequest`: a frozen description of the *whole* fit — formula, model (`meta`/`ttest`), fixed vs random effects, `tau2` method, weights, backend — as one value you can build, inspect, and reuse instead of tracking many keyword arguments. The request below just writes the default out in full so you can see every knob it sets: ::: {#716fa076 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} res2 = group_fit( GroupFitRequest( data=gd, formula="~ 1", model="meta", effects="random", method="pm", ) ) res2.method, res2.estimate[:, 0].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ('pm', array([ 0.412, 0.337, 0.302, 0.256, 0.1 , -0.044])) ``` ::: ::: For everyday analysis, call `fmri_meta`/`fmri_ttest` directly; reach for `group_fit` when a uniform `GroupFitResult` across many fits is worth more than the shorter call. ## Between-Group Meta-Regression To test a group difference, keep the same `fmri_meta` call and just add the covariate to the `formula`. With `method="dl"` this is a *random-effects* meta-regression: it models between-subject heterogeneity (`tau2`) while estimating the group effect. The `C(group)[T.patient]` coefficient is the patient-minus-control contrast per feature. ::: {#7eb544da .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} reg = fmri_meta(gd, formula="~ 1 + C(group)", method="dl") pd.DataFrame({ "feature": reg.feature_names, "patient_minus_ctrl": reg.coefficients[:, 1], "p": reg.p[:, 1], }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
feature patient_minus_ctrl p
0 roi=feature_1 0.453 0.004
1 roi=feature_2 0.299 0.096
2 roi=feature_3 0.138 0.453
3 roi=feature_4 0.276 0.138
4 roi=feature_5 -0.172 0.313
5 roi=feature_6 -0.129 0.461
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Choosing `method` `method` controls how between-subject heterogeneity is handled. Which values are valid depends on whether the formula has a covariate. **One-sample (`formula="~ 1"`):** - `"pm"` (Paule–Mandel), `"reml"` — random effects, iterative `tau2`; the usual choices for a one-sample test. - `"dl"` (DerSimonian–Laird) — random effects, closed-form `tau2`. - `"fe"` — fixed effects: assumes a single true effect with no between-subject variance. **Covariate formula / meta-regression (`formula="~ 1 + …"`):** - `"dl"` — random-effects meta-regression: models `tau2` *and* the covariate. The usual choice, and the one used above. - `"fe"` — fixed-effects meta-regression: the covariate effect with no between-subject variance. - `"pm"` and `"reml"` are intercept-only; passing one a covariate formula raises `NotImplementedError` rather than silently fitting a different model. Rule of thumb: `pm`/`reml` for a one-sample random-effects test, `dl` once the design has a covariate (or `fe` when you specifically want a fixed-effects model). ::: ## One-Sample Test, One Call For a plain one-sample second-level *t*-test, `fmri_ttest` is the typed shortcut — same `GroupData`, a `FmriTTestResult` out. ::: {#1b998e46 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} tt = fmri_ttest(gd, formula="~ 1") type(tt).__name__, tt.engine, tt.statistic.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` ('FmriTTestResult', 'meta', array([ 3.99, 3.75, 3.3 , 2.56, 1.16, -0.5 ])) ``` ::: ::: ## Next - [Functional connectivity](functional-connectivity.qmd) - [Benchmark datasets](benchmark-datasets.qmd)
